Carracele portugheze au fost primele cor: The Portuguese carracks were the first European ships to reach China by sea, and they traded through Macau. In 1592, on her way back from Asia, the “Madre de Deus” was captured by English ships near the Azores and brought to Dartmouth, in England. She was three times bigger than any English ship. On board she had pepper, cloves, cinnamon, pearls, silk and Chinese porcelain: a treasure worth half of England’s royal treasury. The English understood then how rich the trade with Asia was.
Castelele foarte înalte din față și din: The very tall castles at the front and back (like towers) protected her from attacks, but made her hard to handle in a strong wind.

Când apa ține corabia la fel peste tot,: When the water supports the ship equally everywhere, the hull doesn’t bend. On waves, though, it is always bending, one way and then the other. That’s why the keel, the keelson and the long planks have to be very strong.

Cel mai mare curent din lume: curge spre: The biggest current in the world: it flows east, round Antarctica, pushed by the “Roaring Forties”. It helped ships sail towards Australia and Indonesia.

O corabie e o <b>structură</b>, ca un po: A ship is a structure, like a bridge or a building, except that it floats and moves. Weight, water, wind and waves all press on it. Engineers say the parts are under load: some are pulled (tension), some are pressed (compression), and others bend (bending).
A ship can’t sail straight into the wind. She still gets there by zig-zagging: this is called “beating” to windward.
O corabie trebuie să urce <b>6 rânduri</:
A ship has to climb 6 rows up a narrow channel to the harbour straight ahead. The wind blows straight from the harbour, so on each row the ship moves diagonally: one row up and one column to the left or to the right. The channel is only 3 columns wide: there are rocks at the edges. The ship starts in the middle column, and the harbour is in the middle column too.
